name: County of Sacramento v. Lewis
court: Supreme Court of the United States
topic: Fourteenth Amendment substantive due process; death of a motorcycle passenger in a high speed police pursuit; the shocks the conscience test and the purpose to cause harm standard
summary: A sheriff's deputy chased a motorcycle at speeds up to 100 miles per hour through a residential neighborhood; when the motorcycle tipped over, the patrol car skidded into the 16 year old passenger and killed him. The Supreme Court held that there was no Fourth Amendment seizure, so the claim was governed by substantive due process, and that in a high speed chase aimed at apprehending a suspect only a purpose to cause harm unrelated to the legitimate object of arrest shocks the conscience. Deliberate or reckless indifference is not enough. It is taught as the case that sets the constitutional standard for pursuits and that explains when the shocks the conscience test applies.
coverage: The full opinion of the Court by Justice Souter, the syllabus, and the separate opinions of Chief Justice Rehnquist, Justice Kennedy (joined by Justice O'Connor), Justice Breyer, Justice Stevens, and Justice Scalia (joined by Justice Thomas) were read from the Library of Congress U.S. Reports scan at https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/usrep/usrep523/usrep523833/usrep523833.pdf. The scan is headed 523 U.S. 833, No. 96-1337, argued December 9, 1997, decided May 26, 1998, which confirms the citation.
The Ninth Circuit opinion (98 F.3d 434) and the district court ruling were not read. They are described only as the Supreme Court described them.

The agency involved is identified in the opinion as the Sacramento County Sheriff's Department. The guide's agency guardrail concerns a different Sacramento County department and is not implicated by naming the sheriff's department as the Supreme Court did.

Footnote 5 of the opinion, which directed courts to decide the constitutional question before qualified immunity, was later modified by Pearson v. Callahan, 555 U.S. 223 (2009), which permits courts to address the two prongs in either order. Pearson was not read for this brief; the point is stated as the Sixth Circuit summarized it in Hart v. City of Grand Rapids, which was read for a companion brief.
No California proceedings on the state law claims were verified.
facts:
The facts are as the Supreme Court recounted them. On May 22, 1990, at about 8:30 p.m., Sacramento County Sheriff's Deputy James Everett Smith and Officer Murray Stapp responded to a call to break up a fight. Returning to his patrol car, Stapp saw a motorcycle approaching at high speed. It was driven by 18 year old Brian Willard and carried 16 year old Philip Lewis as a passenger. Neither boy had anything to do with the fight.

Stapp turned on his rotating lights, yelled at the boys to stop, and pulled his car closer to Smith's to pen the motorcycle in. Willard slowly maneuvered between the two cars and sped off. Smith immediately activated his emergency lights and siren, made a quick turn, and pursued at high speed. For 75 seconds over 1.3 miles in a residential neighborhood the motorcycle wove in and out of oncoming traffic, forcing two cars and a bicycle off the road. Speeds reached 100 miles per hour, with Smith following as close as 100 feet; at that speed his car would have needed 650 feet to stop.

The chase ended when the motorcycle tipped over as Willard tried a sharp left turn. Smith slammed on his brakes. Willard was out of the way but Lewis was not. The patrol car skidded into Lewis at 40 miles per hour, propelling him about 70 feet down the road and inflicting massive injuries. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

Lewis's parents and estate sued Smith, the county, and the sheriff's department under 42 U.S.C. section 1983, alleging a deprivation of Lewis's Fourteenth Amendment substantive due process right to life, and brought state law claims. The district court granted summary judgment to Smith on qualified immunity, finding no pre 1990 decision establishing a substantive due process right in the pursuit context, and granted summary judgment to the county and department on municipal liability. The Ninth Circuit reversed as to Smith. It held that the appropriate degree of fault for high speed pursuits is deliberate indifference to, or reckless disregard for, a person's right to life, that the law was clearly established, and that Smith's apparent disregard of the department's General Order on pursuits, which required communicating with dispatch and weighing the seriousness of the offense, the need for apprehension, and the hazards of continuing, created a genuine issue of fact. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve a conflict among the circuits on the standard of culpability for pursuit cases.
holding:
Reversed. Justice Souter wrote for the Court, joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justices O'Connor, Kennedy, Ginsburg, and Breyer. The Court held that a police officer does not violate substantive due process by causing death through deliberate or reckless indifference to life in a high speed chase aimed at apprehending a suspected offender; only a purpose to cause harm unrelated to the legitimate object of arrest will satisfy the element of arbitrary conduct shocking to the conscience.

Why not the Fourth Amendment. Graham v. Connor requires that a claim covered by a specific constitutional provision be analyzed under that provision rather than substantive due process. But the Fourth Amendment covers only searches and seizures, and there was no seizure here. Under Hodari D. a pursuit is not a seizure, and under Brower v. County of Inyo a seizure occurs only when freedom of movement is terminated through means intentionally applied. A patrol car that accidentally crashes into a fleeing suspect it was trying to stop by show of authority has not seized him. So substantive due process analysis was available.

The shocks the conscience test. The core of due process is protection against arbitrary government action, and for executive action only the most egregious conduct is arbitrary in the constitutional sense. For half a century the Court has described that level as conduct that shocks the conscience, first in Rochin v. California. The test points clearly away from liability or clearly toward it only at the ends of the culpability spectrum. Negligently inflicted harm is categorically beneath the threshold; conduct intended to injure in some way unjustifiable by any government interest is most likely to shock the conscience. The middle range, recklessness or gross negligence, presents closer calls, and the answer depends on context.

Why deliberate indifference is not enough in a pursuit. The Court had recognized deliberate indifference as sufficient for the medical needs of pretrial detainees, where forethought is feasible and obligatory. But the standard is sensibly employed only when actual deliberation is practical. In Whitley v. Albers the Court had held that in a prison riot, where officials face competing obligations and must act in haste and under pressure, liability turns on whether force was applied maliciously and sadistically for the very purpose of causing harm. The analogy to sudden police chases was hard to avoid. Police on an occasion calling for fast action must act decisively and show restraint at the same moment, balancing the need to stop a suspect against the high speed threat to suspects, passengers, other drivers, and bystanders. When unforeseen circumstances demand an officer's instant judgment, even precipitate recklessness fails to inch close enough to harmful purpose to shock the conscience. "Accordingly, we hold that high-speed chases with no intent to harm suspects physically or to worsen their legal plight do not give rise to liability under the Fourteenth Amendment, redressible by an action under § 1983."

Application. The fault actually claimed against Smith was conscious disregard, which the Court treated as deliberate indifference or reckless disregard. That did not meet the test. The police had done nothing to cause Willard's high speed driving, nothing to excuse his flouting of police authority to control traffic, and nothing beyond a refusal to call off the chase to encourage him. Willard's outrageous behavior was practically instantaneous, and so was Smith's instinctive response. "While prudence would have repressed the reaction, the officer's instinct was to do his job as a law enforcement officer, not to induce Willard's lawlessness, or to terrorize, cause harm, or kill." Whether or not Smith's conduct offended tort law reasonableness or law enforcement's own codes of sound practice, it did not shock the conscience.

The separate opinions. Chief Justice Rehnquist joined the Court and noted that shocks the conscience was the right choice among the alternatives the county had posed. Justice Kennedy, joined by Justice O'Connor, joined the Court and wrote that the phrase must be viewed with skepticism as a subjective sounding standard, that history and tradition are the starting point of the inquiry, and that absent intent to injure police may conduct a dangerous chase of a suspect who disobeys a lawful command to stop; any rule suggesting suspects may ignore a command to stop and then sue might cause more flight. Justice Breyer joined the Court but agreed with Justice Stevens that lower courts should retain flexibility to decide qualified immunity without reaching difficult constitutional questions. Justice Stevens concurred in the judgment only; he would have reinstated the district court's qualified immunity ruling because the law was not clearly established in 1990 and would not have decided the constitutional question. Justice Scalia, joined by Justice Thomas, concurred in the judgment; he criticized the shocks the conscience test as subjective and would have reversed because the plaintiffs offered no textual or historical support for the asserted due process right, noting that California's legislature had chosen to immunize officers in pursuits under Vehicle Code section 17004.
notDecided:
Whether the officer's conduct violated state tort law or departmental policy. The Court said that to say due process is not offended is not to imply anything about the conduct's treatment under state law, and noted California's own rules on pursuit liability, including Vehicle Code section 17004.

Municipal liability. The Ninth Circuit had affirmed summary judgment for the county and the sheriff's department, and that issue was not before the Court.

Whether California's postdeprivation procedures and immunity rules denied the family an adequate remedy. The plaintiffs did not make that argument and the Court expressed no opinion on it.

What standard applies when an officer does have time to deliberate. The Court held that deliberate indifference is the wrong standard for a sudden pursuit because deliberation is not practical; it did not hold that deliberate indifference can never apply to police conduct outside custody. Lower courts, including the Ninth Circuit in later cases, have asked whether actual deliberation was practical to decide which standard governs.

Qualified immunity. The Court decided the constitutional question first and did not reach whether the right was clearly established.
inPractice:
Lewis gives officers two rules. The first is about which constitution applies. When an officer uses force in an arrest, stop, or other seizure, Graham's Fourth Amendment reasonableness test governs. When no seizure has occurred, as with a pursuit that ends in an accidental collision, the claim is substantive due process, and the question is whether the officer's conduct shocks the conscience.

The second rule is what shocks the conscience in a pursuit. The Court held that in a high speed chase aimed at apprehending a suspected offender, where unforeseen circumstances demand instant judgment, only a purpose to cause harm unrelated to the legitimate object of arrest meets the standard. Reckless or deliberately indifferent driving, even driving that violates the department's pursuit policy, does not create federal constitutional liability. The Court said so directly: Smith apparently disregarded the General Order, prudence would have repressed his reaction, and the conduct still did not shock the conscience.

That is not a license. The Court was careful to say the result implies nothing about state law or departmental codes of practice. California has its own pursuit statutes, immunities, and training requirements, and an agency can discipline or terminate for a policy violation that no federal court would touch. The Ninth Circuit has also applied Lewis by asking whether actual deliberation was practical; where it was, the more demanding purpose to harm standard may not apply, and deliberate indifference may suffice.

Dr. Sowards teaches Lewis with Rochin as the two ends of the substantive due process line: Rochin for the origin of the test, Lewis for its limits in fast moving field situations. The training point is that the constitutional floor for pursuits is low because the Court trusts policy, training, and state law to do the real work, and that is exactly where an officer's conduct will be judged.
trainIt:
Teach the two track analysis. Give students a pursuit scenario and change one fact at a time: the officer rams the car intentionally (a seizure, Fourth Amendment, Graham and Scott v. Harris), the officer loses control and strikes a bystander (no seizure, Fourteenth Amendment, Lewis), the officer shoots at the fleeing car (a seizure, Fourth Amendment). Students should be able to say which test applies and why. Lewis supplies the no seizure branch.

Teach the pursuit policy as the operative standard. Lewis listed what the Sacramento County General Order required: notify dispatch, weigh the seriousness of the offense against the risk, consider whether apprehension is necessary, consider the hazards to life and property, and discontinue when hazards outweigh the benefits of immediate apprehension. The Supreme Court held that disregarding those requirements did not violate the Constitution. Use that as the setup for the real lesson: the policy is where the agency, the state, and the public will judge the pursuit, and it should be trained and documented as such.

Teach deliberation as the hinge. The Court distinguished custody, where forethought is feasible and deliberate indifference can shock the conscience, from a sudden chase, where it cannot. Have students identify field situations where time to deliberate exists (a standoff, a planned arrest, a mental health call that has stabilized) and situations where it does not, and explain how the standard shifts. This connects Lewis to the custody and restraint cases in the course.

Teach the dissenting and concurring views briefly: several Justices doubted that shocks the conscience is a usable test. That is why students should rely on policy and state law, which are specific, rather than on the constitutional floor.
caution: Read in full from the Library of Congress scan. Lewis sets the substantive due process standard for a sudden high speed pursuit that does not involve a seizure. It should not be taught as a Fourth Amendment case, as a ruling on state law pursuit liability, or as approval of the deputy's driving; the Court said prudence would have repressed his reaction and that the result implies nothing about state law or departmental standards. The opinion's direction in footnote 5 to decide the constitutional question before qualified immunity was later made discretionary by Pearson v. Callahan.

applications.title: No seizure, no Fourth Amendment
applications.body: A pursuit is not a seizure, and an accidental collision during a pursuit is not a seizure because the stop was not accomplished through means intentionally applied. Claims arising from such collisions are substantive due process claims.

applications.title: Purpose to harm is the standard in a sudden chase
applications.body: In a high speed chase aimed at apprehending a suspect, only a purpose to cause harm unrelated to the legitimate object of arrest shocks the conscience. Reckless or deliberately indifferent driving does not create federal liability.

applications.title: The policy violation did not matter to the Constitution
applications.body: The deputy apparently disregarded the department's General Order on pursuits. The Court held that did not change the result under the Fourteenth Amendment, while saying nothing about state law or discipline. Policy and state law are where pursuit decisions are actually judged.

applications.title: Deliberation changes the standard
applications.body: Deliberate indifference shocks the conscience where officials have time to deliberate, as in custody and medical care. It is not the standard where unforeseen circumstances demand instant judgment. Whether actual deliberation was practical decides which test applies.

applications.title: Flight is the suspect's choice
applications.body: The Court stressed that the police did nothing to cause the motorcyclist's flight and that his lawless driving was practically instantaneous. Justice Kennedy added that any rule letting suspects ignore a lawful command to stop and then sue might cause more flight.

quiz.q: Why was Lewis's death analyzed under substantive due process rather than the Fourth Amendment?
options: Because the officer intended to hit him
Because there was no seizure: a pursuit is not a seizure, and the collision was not a termination of movement through means intentionally applied
Because the Fourth Amendment does not apply to vehicles
quiz.teach: Under Hodari D. and Brower, an accidental collision during a pursuit is not a Fourth Amendment seizure. Graham's more specific provision rule therefore did not bar the due process claim.

quiz.q: What level of culpability did the Court require for substantive due process liability in a high speed chase aimed at apprehending a suspect?
options: A purpose to cause harm unrelated to the legitimate object of arrest
quiz.teach: The Court compared a sudden pursuit to a prison riot under Whitley v. Albers and held that only a purpose to cause harm shocks the conscience when officers must make instant judgments.

quiz.q: What did the Court say about the deputy's apparent violation of the department's pursuit policy?
options: It did not change the due process result, and the Court expressed no view on state law or departmental standards
quiz.teach: The Court said that regardless whether Smith's behavior offended tort law reasonableness or law enforcement's own codes of sound practice, it did not shock the conscience, and that the ruling implied nothing about treatment under state law.
